  1. Estonia's Tax and Customs Board states (page updated 16 September 2026) that from April 2027 VAT payers submit the transaction data behind the VAT return, not the return form, from accounting software or e-MTA; the intra-Community supply report joins the return; invoices under EUR 1,000 and those to private persons 'still need not be declared'. The enacted rewrite of VAT Act § 27 is dated 1 January 2027; the page leaves the three-month gap unexplained. The Board ties mandatory e-invoices to the EU VAT change applying from 1 July 2030; no Estonian act sets a general e-invoice duty earlier as of 5 October 2026, but a registered e-invoice recipient may demand one (Accounting Act § 7^1).

  2. Form TSD is set by Minister of Finance Regulation No 60 of 29 November 2010. Until 4 October 2026 it had a main form and eight annexes: 1 payments to resident natural persons; 2 payments to non-residents; 3 profit taken out of a non-resident's permanent establishment; 4 fringe benefits; 5 gifts, donations, entertainment expenses; 6 non-business expenses, taxation-mismatch amounts; 7 dividends, equity payouts, hidden distributions, CFC profit, exit tax; 8 international sea carriage (3 and 7 also: banks' advance tax). In the text in force from 5 October 2026 (RT I, 02.10.2026, 16) Annex 1 is the 'Payments made to persons' part of form TSD, Annex 2 is repealed; Annexes 3-8 and form INF 1 stay.

  3. Banks are the exception to Estonia's rule of taxing profit only on distribution. Under Income Tax Act § 47^1 a resident credit institution and the Estonian branch of a non-resident one pay an advance income tax by the 10th day of the third month of each quarter on the previous quarter's profit. The rate (§ 4(5)) was 14% from 1 January 2018 to 31 December 2024 and is 18% from 1 January 2025 (RT I, 30.06.2023, 107), in force on 5 October 2026. A draft Riigikogu resolution (1038 OE, introduced by the Centre Party group on 29 September 2026) proposes that the Government change the taxation of bank profits; it is a proposal to the Government, not a bill, and is not adopted.

  4. Estonia taxes a loan to a shareholder as a hidden profit distribution where the facts point that way. Under Income Tax Act § 50^2 (in force since 1 January 2018, act published RT I, 07.07.2017, 3) a resident company pays income tax on a loan given to its shareholder, partner or member 'if the circumstances of the transaction indicate that it may be a hidden profit distribution'. For a loan to a parent company or to a fellow subsidiary (other than the lender's own subsidiary) with a repayment term longer than 48 months, the taxpayer must, at the tax authority's request, prove the ability and intention to repay, with at least 30 days to produce evidence. In force 5 October 2026.

  5. The OECD Multilateral Instrument did not change the company tie-breaker of the Estonia–Cyprus tax convention. The synthesised text prepared jointly by the two competent authorities (Estonia's Ministry of Finance, late 2021) inserts only three MLI provisions — Art. 6(1) (preamble), the first sentence of Art. 16(1) (mutual agreement procedure) and Art. 7(1) (principal purposes test) — and reproduces Art. 4(3) unchanged. Per its footnotes these apply for taxes withheld at source from 1 January 2022 in both states, and for other taxes for taxable periods beginning on or after 1 January 2023 in Estonia and 25 June 2022 in Cyprus; the Ministry's table shows only 'MLI effective from 01.01.2022'.

The Estonian Tax and Customs Board's e-services environment e-MTA accepts login with other EEA states' eIDs: its page for foreigners (last updated 19 February 2026) says a foreigner can enter with 'the European Union digital identity card (eID)', an Estonian ID-card (including an e-resident's digital ID) or Estonian Mobile-ID or Smart-ID, and its list of eID tools 'with a high assurance level' names 23 states, among them 'Cyprus — Cyprus National eID — IDMe.cy'. On first entry by 'EU eID' a user account is created and customer support then opens the e-services; a legal representative needing access on behalf of a company must ask the Board separately.

  7. Estonia has no annual corporate income tax return. The Tax and Customs Board states: 'Estonia does not have a corporate tax return covering the taxable income of the entire calendar year'; a company declares income tax, social tax, funded pension contributions and unemployment insurance premiums on the monthly form TSD, and where it made no taxable payments in a month and has no information to submit 'there is no need to file TSD tax returns containing only zeros'. A TSD is still due without tax where, for example, a taxable payment yields zero tax or a contribution to equity is paid in (Annex 7). A VAT-registered company, by contrast, files a VAT return even with no supply in the period.

  8. Fees an Estonian OÜ pays its board member are taxed in Estonia even when the member lives abroad (Estonian texts in force on 5 October 2026). Income Tax Act § 29(2) taxes income a non-resident receives for performing the duties of a member of the management or controlling body of a resident legal person; the company withholds the tax (§ 41 point 2) at the § 4(1) rate, 22% (§ 43(1) point 1), final for the non-resident (§ 43(4)) unless a tax treaty sets a lower rate (§ 43(2)). Social Tax Act § 2(1) point 4 puts social tax on such fees, at 33% (§ 7(1)); per the Tax and Customs Board it is not due only if the recipient holds an A1 certificate of social security coverage from his home country.

  9. A natural person is an Estonian tax resident if his or her place of residence is in Estonia or if he or she stays in Estonia for at least 183 days in a period of 12 consecutive calendar months; the person counts as resident from the day of arrival (Income Tax Act § 6(1)). A resident is taxed on worldwide income, a non-resident only on the Estonian-source income listed in § 29 (§ 6(1), (3)). The person must tell the tax authority of circumstances that change residence and fill in the residence form (form R) (§ 6(6)); a treaty tie-breaker prevails over the statutory test (§ 6(5)). e-Residency is a digital identity and is not among the tests. In force 5 October 2026.

  10. Estonia has no unconditional duty to issue e-invoices between businesses as of 5 October 2026, but a buyer can impose one. Accounting Act § 7(5) says a source document must be machine-processable, yet allows another written form where a party cannot handle such documents without disproportionate cost. Under § 7^1(3) and (7), in force since 1 July 2025 (act RT I, 10.10.2024, 1), an accounting entity that wants only machine-processable invoices is marked in the commercial register as an e-invoice recipient and may then require the seller to present one; an e-invoice meeting standard EN 16931-1 is presumed proper; parties may agree another standard. The text enacted for 2027 keeps § 7^1.

  11. Art. 15 of the Estonia–Cyprus tax convention (Directors' fees) lets the company's state tax a board member resident in the other state: 'Directors' fees and other similar payments derived by a resident of a Contracting State in his capacity as a member of the board of directors or any other similar organ of a company which is a resident of the other Contracting State may be taxed in that other State.' So Estonia's domestic rule taxing a non-resident board member's fee from an Estonian company (Income Tax Act § 29(2)) is not switched off by the treaty for a Cyprus resident; 'may be taxed' does not make the taxation exclusive.

  12. Estonian tax acts do not oblige a café to run a cash register, but the Alcohol Act does once it sells alcohol (texts in force on 5 October 2026). Value-Added Tax Act § 37(3): an invoice meeting § 37 need not be issued for a supply to a natural person for personal use (three listed cases excepted). The Value-Added Tax, Income Tax and Consumer Protection Acts do not mention a cash register. Alcohol Act § 44 permits retail sale of alcoholic drinks in a shop or catering establishment only where a cash register is on the premises and records every such sale; Taxation Act § 70(1) point 4 and (2) lets the tax authority demand installation where a law obliges it.

  13. A sole proprietor (FIE) in Estonia pays income tax at 22% on business income after deductible expenses and social tax at 33% on the same net income, the latter with a floor and a cap: at least twelve times the monthly rate a year (EUR 886 a month in 2026) and at most ten times the sum of the monthly minimum wages of the year (Social Tax Act § 2(1) point 5, § 2(5)). Social tax is paid in quarterly advances by the 15th day of the third month of each quarter, each equal to three monthly rates x 33%, with the balance due by 1 October of the following year (§ 9(3)). A sole proprietor is not covered by unemployment insurance. In force 5 October 2026.

  14. From 2018 to 2024 Estonia taxed regular dividends at a lower corporate rate: the part of a calendar year's distributed profit not exceeding the average of the previous three calendar years' taxed distributions bore 14% with divisor 0.86 (14/86) (Income Tax Act § 4(5) and § 50^1, in force 1 January 2018, act RT I, 07.07.2017, 3). 2018 was the first year counted, so the rate first applied in 2019, to one third of the profit distributed in 2018 (§ 61(53)). On such a dividend paid to a natural person, resident or non-resident, the company withheld a further 7% (§ 4(4), § 18(1^3), § 29(7^1), § 41 point 7^2). The act of 20 June 2023 (RT I, 30.06.2023, 107) repealed these rules from 1 January 2025.

  15. Personal income tax in Estonia is a flat 22% in 2026 (20% from 2015 to 2024; 22% from 1 January 2025), with 10% on certain pension and insurance payouts (Income Tax Act § 4(1)-(2)). A resident natural person files a return for the year by 30 April of the next year, unless income did not exceed the basic exemption or no further tax is due (§ 44(6); sole proprietors and some others must still file, § 44(6^1)); the pre-filled return opens on 15 February (§ 44(1), (1^1)); tax assessed is due by 1 October (§ 46(3)). A non-resident files only for income from which tax was not withheld under § 41; withheld tax is final unless the income came through an Estonian permanent establishment (§ 43(4)).

  16. To declare a payment to a non-resident - on form TSD or, for dividend recipients, on form INF 1 - an Estonian company needs the recipient's Estonian code: a personal identification code, a registry code or, failing those, a non-resident code issued by the Tax and Customs Board. The recipient or the payer applies for it; the Board says it issues the code 'within 10 days'. An e-resident already has an Estonian personal identification code. The code does not open treaty rates: for those the Board must also hold a certificate of residence from the foreign tax authority (form TM3 or equivalent), valid 12 months for a natural person and 36 for a legal person. Read 5 October 2026.

Cross-border VAT schemes in Estonia as of 5 October 2026: (1) a seller established only in Estonia may keep Estonian VAT on distance sales of goods and telecom and electronic services to consumers in other member states while these stay within EUR 10,000 in the previous and current year (Value-Added Tax Act § 10^1(7)-(9)); otherwise it may use the OSS scheme via e-MTA - quarterly, return and payment by the end of the next month (IOSS: monthly); (2) since 1 January 2025 an Estonian business with Union turnover up to EUR 100,000 may, after notifying the Estonian tax authority, use another member state's small-enterprise exemption within that state's threshold (§ 19^1), reporting quarterly.

  18. An Estonian company does not apply separately to be registered as a taxpayer - a reading of § 18(1) of the Taxation Act as in force on 5 October 2026, not a sentence of it. It lists who must register with the Tax and Customs Board before starting activity in Estonia; of Estonian legal persons it names only one 'that is not entered in the commercial register, the register of non-profit associations and foundations or the register of religious associations' (p 1; the other points cover public agencies, non-residents and associations without legal personality). An OÜ, being in the commercial register, is thus outside the duty. VAT registration is a separate step under the Value-Added Tax Act.

The Estonian Tax and Customs Board's comparison of business forms (page last updated 14 May 2026, read 5 October 2026): an entrepreneur-account holder files no returns and cannot deduct expenses, and 'currently, entrepreneur accounts can only be opened at the LHV Pank'; a sole proprietor (FIE) reports once a year on income tax return form E, may deduct business expenses and pays advance social tax of EUR 877.14 per quarter in 2026; an OÜ files monthly returns (TSD, KMD, KMD INF) and an annual report to the Business Register.   20. Estonia transposed DAC7 (platform reporting) as chapter 2^4 of the Tax Information Exchange Act, in force since 1 January 2023 (act published RT I, 29.12.2022, 1). An Estonian-resident platform operator identifies reportable sellers by 31 December and reports them to the tax authority by 31 January of the next year; reportable activities are renting immovable property, time- or task-based services, sale of goods and renting means of transport. Among the sellers excluded (§ 20^22(3)): one with fewer than 30 sales of goods and at most EUR 2,000 of consideration in the year. Software that only enables payment processing, listing or advertising, or redirecting users is no platform (§ 20^20(2)).

A management board member's fee paid by an Estonian company bears income tax (22%, withheld) and social tax (33%, paid by the company) and, for a resident in the second pension pillar, the funded pension contribution, but no unemployment insurance premium: a board member outside the Employment Contracts Act is not insured. Social tax falls on the fee actually paid: the monthly minimum base of Social Tax Act § 2(2) names employees and officials, and the Tax and Customs Board's example of an e-resident board member on EUR 100 a month gives EUR 22 income tax, EUR 33 social tax, company cost EUR 133. Bases: Income Tax Act § 13(2), § 41; Social Tax Act § 2(1) p 4; Unemployment Insurance Act § 3.

No general duty to install a cash register was found in Estonia's Taxation Act on 5 October 2026: § 70(1) point 4 only lets the tax authority demand that a taxpayer install 'devices enabling the monitoring of cash settlements, including a cash register', and § 70(2) allows that demand where the taxpayer has not met a duty to install such a device imposed on it by law.   29. A fee paid by an Estonian company to a board member who is not an Estonian resident is taxed in Estonia wherever the work is done. Income Tax Act § 29(2) taxes a non-resident's income for performing the duties of a member of the management or supervisory body of a resident legal person; § 41 point 2 makes the company withhold. The Tax and Customs Board's page for e-residents' companies (4 November 2025) says the company 'must pay income tax and social tax in Estonia regardless of the location where work is carried on', reports the fee on form TSD (the page names Annex 2, dropped from the form in October 2026) and registers a member with a fee taxable in Estonia in the employment register.

Estonia's entrepreneur account (ettevõtluskonto), under the Simplified Business Income Taxation Act in force since 1 January 2018: a natural person may open, with a credit institution resident in an EEA state, an account that receives only proceeds from services and sales of goods; the bank reserves and transfers the tax. The holder may not be registered for VAT nor act as a sole proprietor in the same or a similar field (§ 2(2)). As of 5 October 2026 the rate is 20% of the sums received (§ 4(1), in force from 1 January 2025), plus the funded-pension contribution rate for persons obliged to pay it; until 31 December 2024 it was 20% up to EUR 25,000 per calendar year and 40% on the excess.

The personal basic exemption in Estonia became a flat amount on 1 January 2026: § 23(1) of the Income Tax Act deducts EUR 8,400 a year from a resident natural person's income (EUR 700 a month), the earlier sliding scale being repealed. Until then the exemption was EUR 7,848 a year and shrank by formula once annual income exceeded EUR 14,400 (wording in force from 1 January 2023). The flat amount was enacted by the Act of 20 June 2023 (RT I, 30.06.2023, 107) for an earlier date; its entry into force was changed to 1 January 2026 by the Act of 4 December 2024 (RT I, 20.12.2024, 2). It does not apply from the tax period in which the person reaches pension age.

  32. The Security Tax Act never applied to income or profit. An act adopted on 18 June 2025 (RT I, 08.07.2025, 1, in force 18 July 2025) repealed it before its income and profit parts were due to start on 1 January 2026; of its provisions only the VAT amendments of 1 July 2025 had taken effect.   33. The lower corporate rate for regular dividends existed for seven years. From 1 January 2018 (RT I, 07.07.2017, 3) § 4(5) of the Income Tax Act taxed profit distributed under § 50^1 at 14%, the taxable amount being divided by 0.86, and § 4(4) set a 7% rate on such dividends in a natural person's hands. Both went on 1 January 2025 under the Act of 20 June 2023 (RT I, 30.06.2023, 107), which also raised the general rate to 22%; § 4(5) in force on 5 October 2026 keeps only an 18% rate for § 47^1. A remnant stays: under § 61(68) a resident company still withholds 7% on a dividend paid to a natural person that is exempt under § 50(1^1) if the underlying profit was taxed under the old § 50^1.

  34. Estonian social tax on an employee has a floor. Under Social Tax Act § 2(2) it is paid on the remuneration paid to an employee or official for a month 'but not on less than the monthly rate' of § 2^1, set yearly by the State Budget Act, not below the minimum wage of 1 July of the previous year. For 2026 it is EUR 886 (State Budget Act § 2(6), text RT I, 03.07.2026, 24) - a minimum social tax of EUR 292.38 a month, per the Tax and Customs Board (2025: EUR 820 and EUR 270.60; 2024: EUR 725 and EUR 239.25). § 2(3) scales the floor to time worked; § 2(4) lifts it in listed cases. § 2(2) names employees and officials, not board members: a Board example taxes a EUR 100 monthly board fee at 33%.

The Estonian Social Insurance Board (page updated 11 March 2026) on which state insures a person tied to more than one EU or EEA state or Switzerland: one state's legislation applies at a time; for work in several states the place of a substantial part of the activity decides, and if that is the state of residence, its scheme applies. A person living in Estonia and working in several states applies to the Board for Form A1; one who works in Estonia too but lives elsewhere applies in the state of residence. An A1 comes 'within the next working day' only on an electronic application meeting listed conditions (one: residence in Estonia), else within 30 days. Board members are not mentioned.

  39. An Estonian company that is not VAT-registered still meets VAT when it buys services from abroad. Under Value-Added Tax Act § 21(1) an Estonian person receiving, from a foreign business not registered for VAT in Estonia, a service listed in § 10(5) - among them advertising, consultancy, accounting, legal, data-processing, financial and electronically supplied services - must register as a 'taxable person with limited liability' from the day the service is received, applying within three working days (§ 21(3)), and pays the VAT on such services itself (§ 3(5)).   45. A café must give each paying consumer a proof of purchase. Consumer Protection Act § 4(4), as worded from 1 September 2025 (RT I, 08.07.2025, 71), obliges a trader to present the consumer a document proving the purchase when goods or a service are paid for at once; it shows at least the trader's name and place of business, the date, and each item's name, price and the amount paid (§ 4(4^1)). A paper document is given on the consumer's demand, and by default when the consumer pays in cash and uses no customer card giving electronic access to the purchase document (§ 4(4^2)). Until 31 August 2025, § 4(5) said that below EUR 20 the document was given on request; that subsection was repealed.

  102. The Estonia–Cyprus tax convention removes double taxation by different methods on each side (Art. 21). Estonia exempts: where a resident of Estonia derives income which under the convention 'has been taxed in Cyprus', Estonia exempts it, and may take it into account when computing tax on the rest. Cyprus credits: 'subject to the provisions of Cyprus Tax Law regarding credit for foreign tax', Estonian tax paid in accordance with the convention on income derived from Estonia is allowed as a credit against Cyprus tax, capped at the Cyprus tax on that income. For a Cyprus resident's board fee taxed in Estonia under Art. 15, the relief therefore lies with Cyprus.

  105. A business must register for Estonian VAT once its turnover with place of supply in Estonia exceeds EUR 40,000 in a calendar year; the duty arises that day (Value-Added Tax Act § 19(1), in force 5 October 2026). Since 1 January 2025 the turnover counted is that of § 19^1(3): taxable supplies incl. zero-rated, real-estate, insurance and financial services, less sales of fixed assets and incidental transactions. No duty arises if the year's turnover is all exempt and zero-rated supply (other than intra-Community supply of goods). A foreign business with no fixed establishment in Estonia has no threshold: it registers from its first taxable supply the customer does not reverse-charge (§ 19(3)).

The person providing work - an Estonian or a non-resident legal person, among others - must register each worker in the employment register kept by the Tax and Customs Board no later than the moment work starts; suspension and termination within ten days (Taxation Act § 25^2). The register covers persons whose work creates a tax liability in Estonia - employees, service providers under a contract under the law of obligations, members of a legal person's management or supervisory body - and persons working unpaid in a company's economic interests (§ 25^1(4)-(5)). Channels: e-MTA, X-tee, a service bureau; by phone or SMS only the start, to be completed within seven calendar days (§ 25^4(3)).

  109. A transitional rule keeps one trace of Estonia's former lower dividend rate alive in 2026: under Income Tax Act § 61(68) a resident company withholds 7% from a dividend or other profit distribution paid to a natural person where that dividend is exempt at company level under § 50(1^1) and the underlying profit was taxed under the 14/86 rule in force until 31 December 2024. The Tax and Customs Board adds that such a dividend may be passed on tax-free to a corporate shareholder if the company passing it on held at least 10% of the payer when it received it, and that a tax treaty may free a non-resident natural person from the 7% (Cyprus is on the Board's list) or cut it to 5%.

How payment of an Estonian OÜ's capital is shown to the registrar, as of 5 October 2026: a notice from a credit institution or payment institution is attached to the registration application only if the contribution exceeds EUR 50,000; where the cash contribution is not over EUR 50,000 the management board members confirm in the application that the contributions have been paid to the company (Commercial Code § 144(1) 3) and § 144(2¹), in force from 1 February 2023). Under § 520(4) the payment account the founders open in the name of the company being founded may be with a credit or payment institution established in any EEA state or its branch in an EEA state (wording of 1 January 2019).

  16. An Estonian company must appoint a contact person in Estonia when its address is in a foreign state (Commercial Register Act § 24(2), in force since 1 February 2023).   17. Estonia's contact-person rule in three dated versions. Until 14 January 2018 Commercial Code § 63¹(2) made an OÜ name a person with an Estonian address for service if at least half of its board members did not reside in Estonia, another EEA state or Switzerland. From 15 January 2018 (RT I, 20.04.2017, 1) a 'contact person' was compulsory when the management board 'is located in a foreign state'; only listed professionals could be appointed, but a board member, shareholder or procurator residing in Estonia could also be (§ 63¹(3)). From 1 February 2023 § 63¹ was repealed; § 24 of the Commercial Register Act ties the duty to the legal person's address being abroad and has no such exception.

Deletion of an Estonian company for a missing annual report, in force since 1 February 2023: after the legal deadline the registrar sets a time limit for filing with a warning of deletion, which may be sent automatically; the company may be deleted if it has not filed within that limit and at least three months have passed since the statutory filing date (Commercial Register Act § 61). Deletion also requires that the registers show no assets, that no court, criminal or enforcement proceedings are pending, consent of the authorities named by the minister, and a notice in Ametlikud Teadaanded at least three months before (§ 60(2), (5)). Restoration can be sought within three years (§ 64(2)).

  21. E-invoicing in Estonia in two dated versions of § 7¹ of the Accounting Act. From 1 July 2019 (RT I, 15.03.2019, 3) a seller had to present a machine-readable invoice (e-invoice) when supplying the state, local authorities, legal persons in public law and entities they control. From 1 July 2025 (RT I, 10.10.2024, 1) any accounting entity that wants to receive only e-invoices has itself marked as an e-invoice recipient in the commercial register, and such a buyer may require the seller to present an e-invoice, presumed proper if it meets European standard EN 16931-1 unless the parties agree another standard. The Act lays down no general duty to issue e-invoices to every business customer.

A share-capital contribution paid as a deposit to the registrar's account when an Estonian company is founded must be claimed back: the company applies, no later than one year after its registration, for the money to be returned to its payment account with a credit or payment institution established in an EEA state or a branch there; after that the contribution stays in state revenue.   29. Deleting an Estonian company for a missing annual report became faster on 1 February 2023. Under Commercial Code § 60 (in force until 31 January 2023) the registrar acted once the report was six months overdue, set a time limit of at least six months with a warning of deletion, could then publish a notice in Ametlikud Teadaanded inviting creditors to seek liquidation within six months, and only then delete. From 1 January 2011 an Estonian private limited company (osaühing) could be founded without paying in its share capital: § 140^1 of the Commercial Code (inserted by RT I 2010, 77, 589) let founders, if all natural persons and planned capital up to EUR 25,000, agree that shares need not be paid for on foundation. The contact-person duty for Estonian companies run from abroad dates from 15 January 2018: § 63^1 of the Commercial Code (added by RT I, 20.04.2017, 1) made a company whose management board 'is located in a foreign state' appoint a contact person in Estonia - only a notary, advocate, law office, sworn auditor, audit firm, non-resident's tax representative or trust and company service provider (until 20 July 2020 also a notary's office) - unless a board member, shareholder or procurist living in Estonia took it.   53. The name step in Estonia involves no compulsory prior approval. The e-Business Register's 'Name search' shows identical and similar registered names and trademarks; per the Centre of Registers it 'does not give a definite answer' - the registrar decides during registration. By law a company's business name must be clearly distinguishable from names entered or reserved in the Estonian commercial register, carry 'osaühing' or 'OÜ' at its beginning or end, and be written in the Estonian-Latin alphabet (Commercial Code § 9(2)-(4), § 11(2), § 12(8)). Since 1 March 2024 a person may reserve one name for six months, for a stated legal form and field of activity, for a EUR 150 state fee (§ 15¹).

Outside the expedited procedure the founding documents of an Estonian OÜ go through a notary: the memorandum of association and the articles approved with it must be notarially authenticated and signed by all founders, a representative needs a notarially certified power of attorney, and a sole founder signs a notarially authenticated foundation resolution instead (Commercial Code § 138(4)-(5)).   55. An Estonian OÜ may be founded by one or more persons, natural or legal (Commercial Code § 137). Its management board has one or more members; a member must be a natural person with active legal capacity and need not be a shareholder (§ 180(2)). The Code's part on the OÜ (§§ 135-220), as in force on 5 October 2026, sets no condition of Estonian residence or of nationality for a founder or board member. § 180(3)-(3¹) bars from the board: supervisory board members; persons the articles exclude; persons under a court ban on acting as a board member or on business; persons forbidden to act in the company's field of activity; and persons barred from board membership by law or court decision.

Time limit in the law for an Estonian commercial register entry, as in force on 5 October 2026: an application is reviewed within five working days of its arrival (Commercial Register Act § 41(3)); the period restarts when the application is amended or a further document is filed, runs again for five working days after defects are remedied (§ 41(4)), and the registrar may extend it up to three months for circumstances needing special verification (§ 41(5)). In Estonia's expedited procedure an OÜ uses standard articles of association laid down by ministerial regulation; they replace both the memorandum of association and ordinary articles, state the share capital as a fixed amount, are digitally signed by all founders, and the company cannot add provisions of its own to them (Commercial Code § 139¹(1)-(4), in force since 1 January 2007). A company in a field of activity where the law requires additional data in the articles cannot use them (§ 139¹(5)).

  10. Estonia's right to a basic payment account sits in § 710^1 of the Law of Obligations Act, there since 10 January 2017 (RT I, 31.12.2016, 1); text read: version in force from 1 September 2026. A credit institution must provide basic payment services to 'a consumer who lawfully resides in the European Union' and, 'in the case of justified interest of a consumer', conclude a basic payment service contract; it answers within ten settlement days and must refuse on the grounds of § 42(1) of the AML act. The right belongs to consumers only: a company has no basic-account right, and § 733^14(6) lets even the general duty to contract of § 710^1(1) be excluded for non-consumers.

  14. A Government bill pending in the Riigikogu on 5 October 2026 would spell out who may pull bank-account data. Bill 924 SE, initiated on 21 May 2026, amends the Taxation Act, the AML act and the act implementing the Code of Civil Procedure and the Code of Enforcement Procedure: per its official summary it specifies the rights of the Tax and Customs Board and the Financial Intelligence Unit to obtain data 'above all on bank accounts and account data', states expressly that the tax authority may demand information from credit institutions in tax proceedings, banking secrecy included, and specifies which data it may ask through the Enforcement Register channel. First reading ended 8 June 2026.

Since 15 July 2025 (RT I, 08.07.2025, 4) an Estonian bank may not refuse a consumer a basic payment account because of its risk appetite: § 710^1(5^1) of the Law of Obligations Act says it 'may not refuse to enter into a basic payment service contract on the basis of the risk appetite' set under § 10 of the AML act, but may mitigate risk by capping monthly payments, single transactions and the balance, and by restricting cash withdrawals outside the EEA; the limits do not cover payments of taxes, fines or state fees and may not make the account unusable. Proof of justified interest 'must not be unreasonably burdensome' (2^1); in a dispute the bank bears the burden of proof (14).

  21. Estonia's bank-account register function is carried by the Enforcement Register (täitmisregister) of § 63 of the Code of Enforcement Procedure. § 81 of the AML act obliges every credit and financial institution that opens an IBAN payment account or lets a safe-deposit box to make available through that register the holder's name, personal or registry code and address, the persons authorised to use the account, the holder's beneficial owner, and the IBAN with opening and closing dates - for open accounts and those closed in the previous five years. The duty applies since 10 September 2020 (§ 104^2), first via the electronic seizure system and since 1 January 2024 via the Enforcement Register.

The e-Residency programme describes Estonian banks' practice towards companies of non-residents (knowledge-base article updated 6 October 2025): banks 'will likely consider' either a company with 'a strong connection to Estonia' — employees in Estonia, partners and suppliers there, serving the Estonian market — or a single-shareholder company with easily traceable income; 'a personal visit to their office in Estonia is most likely required'. It also states that 'Estonian companies are not obligated to have a bank account in Estonia or use an Estonian (EE) IBAN for their business transactions', and names LHV as the Estonian bank most used by e-residents.

  48. Estonian tax law does not tie tax payment to an Estonian bank account. The Tax and Customs Board's page 'Payment of taxes' (last updated 21.07.2026) has taxes paid by bank transfer, with the taxpayer's reference number, to its own accounts at SEB Pank, Swedbank, Luminor Bank, LHV Pank and Coop Pank, or in the e-MTA portal by credit card or bank link. For refunds the Taxation Act § 106 (text in force from 1 October 2026) requires only 'the taxpayer's bank account details' and expressly foresees an account abroad: when the refund is transferred 'to the taxpayer's bank account located in a foreign state' the authority may deduct the transfer costs from the refunded sum (§ 106(4)).

A citizen of another EU state who actually lives in Estonia is outside e-Residency: the Police and Border Guard Board issues 'an ID card … to a citizen of the European Union residing in Estonia on the basis of the right of residence', valid for up to five years and not valid as a travel document (page read 5 October 2026), and under § 20⁵(1) of the Identity Documents Act an e-resident's card goes only to a foreign citizen without a valid Estonian identity card or residence permit card. That ordinary ID card is one of the Estonian tools the e-Business Register accepts for signing; an EU citizen living elsewhere has no claim to it.

The e-resident's card gives no right to any service: under § 20^10(1) of Estonia's Identity Documents Act, in force since 1 December 2014 and unchanged on 5 October 2026, a provider of a public or private service may decide to provide a service to an e-resident with the card or to refuse it, may limit the service, and may set additional requirements for access, including additional data and documents or personal appearance at the provider's location. For a public service such limits may be set in two cases: to ensure purposeful use of the card, including preventing offences, or the functioning or safe use of the service (§ 20^10(2)). That a bank is such a private provider is our reading.

  5. An Estonian e-Residency card must be collected in person, because fingerprints are taken at collection: it is not posted, not handed to a representative and not issued by honorary consuls. On 5 October 2026 the programme's list of pick-up locations had no location in Cyprus; it listed Athens (Greece), Tel Aviv (Israel), Cairo (Egypt) and Ankara (Türkiye) among others, and four service offices in Estonia (Tallinn, Tartu, Pärnu, Narva). The programme says a kit not collected within six months of arriving is returned to Estonia and destroyed; the Police and Border Guard Board's FAQ says a longer period can usually be agreed with the pick-up location for good reason.

  6. e-Residency was created by the Act amending the Identity Documents Act and the State Fees Act, adopted by the Riigikogu on 21 October 2014 (RT I, 29.10.2014, 1) and in force from 1 December 2014. It added the e-resident's digital identity card to the Identity Documents Act and set the state fee for reviewing an application at EUR 50. The Police and Border Guard Board, which issues the card, describes it as a digital document usable only for identification and digital signature in an electronic environment and states that it 'does not grant the right to reside in Estonia'.

Applications for an e-resident's digital ID from citizens of twelve states are reviewed only under listed exceptions, per the Police and Border Guard Board (page read 5 October 2026), which cites Identity Documents Act § 20^6(1^1) and covers applications submitted after 1 October 2025. Group I - Afghanistan, Burkina Faso, Iran, Yemen, DR Congo, North Korea, South Sudan, Mali, Nigeria, Syria: reviewed if, among other grounds, the applicant has lived three years running in the EEA, the UK or Switzerland on a residence permit or has permanent economic activity in Estonia. Group II - Belarus and Russia: only if the applicant already held such an ID and has permanent economic activity in Estonia.

  18. A founder living outside Estonia can get an Estonian means of digital signature through the e-resident's digital ID. Per the Police and Border Guard Board (pages read 5 October 2026) it may be granted to a foreign national with a justified interest in Estonian e-services who has no Estonian residence permit, right of residence or identity card and whose citizenship is not under application restrictions; the online application needs a copy of the travel document, a photo, a CV and a payment card; state fee EUR 150, not refunded on refusal; decision within 30 days; the card reaches the pick-up location 2-5 weeks later and is collected in person. It serves only to identify and sign.

  19. The Act of 4 June 2025 amending Estonia's Identity Documents Act (RT I, 26.06.2025, 1) also changed e-Residency vetting from 6 July 2025. The Financial Intelligence Unit joined the Police and Border Guard Board (PPA), the Security Police and the Tax and Customs Board as a body supervising the use of e-resident cards (§ 20^8(1)) and may process data from the application procedure and on the card's use (§ 20^8(2^1)). The application is now submitted personally in the PPA's self-service (§ 20^7(1^1)); the wording in force until 5 July 2025 let a person file with an Estonian consular officer. Suspension of a card's certificates left the Act on 15 November 2025; revocation remains.

  20. Recognition of electronic signatures between Member States is a separate rule of Regulation (EU) No 910/2014 (consolidated version of 18 October 2024), apart from the login duty of Art. 6. Art. 24a(1): qualified electronic signatures based on a qualified certificate issued in one Member State 'shall be recognised' as such 'in all other Member States'. Art. 27(1)–(2): a Member State requiring an advanced electronic signature for an online public-sector service must recognise advanced and qualified signatures 'in at least the formats or using methods defined in the implementing acts'. Whether the Estonian e-Business Register's signing step takes a foreign qualified signature was not tested.

  21. The legal basis of Estonian e-Residency is chapter 5² of the Identity Documents Act (Isikut tõendavate dokumentide seadus). The chapter was inserted as §§ 20⁵–20¹¹ by the act published as RT I, 29.10.2014, 1, in force since 1 December 2014; § 20¹² was added from 1 April 2015 (RT I, 23.03.2015, 1). Under § 20⁵(1), in the wording in force since 6 July 2025, the e-resident's digital identity card is a digital document issued to a citizen of a foreign state who holds no valid Estonian identity card or residence permit card and is not applying for one at the same time. Estonian text read, version in force from 1 October 2026 (RT I, 30.06.2026, 53).

Finantsinspektsioon's advisory guidelines on preventing money laundering (version valid from 1 May 2024, point 6.3.2) give a credit or financial institution 'the right to cancel the long-term contract serving as a basis for a business relationship extraordinarily and without notice' where issue of the person's e-resident digital identity card is refused, its validity is suspended or it is declared invalid under § 20^6(2) or (3) of the Identity Documents Act. AS SEB Pank's General Terms valid as of 01.06.2026 list the same event among grounds for extraordinary cancellation without notice (clause 118.28).

  47. A bill pending in the Riigikogu on 5 October 2026 would end the in-person card pick-up for Estonian e-Residency. Bill 905 SE, amending the Identity Documents Act, was initiated by the Government on 7 May 2026; its first reading was on the plenary agenda of 1 June 2026 and it stood at the second-reading stage, not adopted. Per the Riigikogu's summary, e-residents' identity would be verified remotely by biometrics from March 2027, and from March 2028 a card-free 'e-identification means' would replace the digital ID card, the right to use it granted by the Police and Border Guard Board. The bill's § 9 sets 2 March 2027 and 1 March 2028 for the main provisions.

An Estonian bank must refuse or end a relationship it cannot vet: § 42 of the AML act (in force 21 July 2026) forbids establishing a business relationship when the bank is unable to apply due diligence or suspects money laundering, and treats a customer's refusal to give information or documents as a fundamental breach obliging the bank to terminate extraordinarily and report to the Financial Intelligence Unit. § 43(2) adds a ground specific to e-residents: the bank may terminate 'extraordinarily and without advance notification' when an e-resident's digital identity card is refused, suspended or declared invalid under § 20^6(2) or (3) of the Identity Documents Act.

A cash ceiling will reach Estonian merchants through EU law: Article 80 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 lets persons trading in goods or providing services accept or make a cash payment 'only up to an amount of EUR 10 000', in one operation or several linked ones, and the regulation applies from 10 July 2027 (Article 90). Member States may set lower limits after consulting the European Central Bank; none was found in Estonian law on 5 October 2026. Estonia's AML act (§ 19(1), in force 21 July 2026) requires due diligence when a business relationship is established, for an occasional transaction from EUR 15,000, when earlier data are in doubt and on any suspicion of money laundering. The six measures of § 20(1): identify the customer and verify the data from a reliable independent source; identify the representative and his powers; identify the beneficial owner and understand the ownership and control structure; understand the purpose of the relationship; establish whether the person is politically exposed; monitor the relationship. Measures 1-5 precede the relationship 'unless otherwise provided' (§ 19(5)); § 27 has the exceptions.

Records under Estonia's AML act (§ 47, in force 21 July 2026): identification documents or their copies, registered data and the documents on which the business relationship was founded are kept five years after the relationship ends (Estonian text; the translation adds 'no less than'); transaction documents and the data behind a report to the Financial Intelligence Unit for at least five years after the transaction or report. Copies need not be kept if the person was identified by electronic identification and trust services or the document stays available in a state database. The data are deleted when the term ends; a supervisor's precept may extend retention by at most five more years.

Estonia's AML act tells a bank to decide in writing whom it will not serve. § 10 (text of 21 July 2026) defines 'risk appetite' as the exposure the obliged entity is prepared to assume, set by senior management in writing; it must name at least the kinds of persons with whom it wishes to avoid business relationships (§ 10(3)), and the management board of a credit or financial institution also decides whether to deal with persons from outside the EEA (§ 10(4)). The original 2017 text of § 10(4) added 'or with e-residents'; the amendment in force 10 September 2020 (RT I, 10.07.2020, 1) deleted those words. A refusal on this ground is a policy the act makes the bank set, not a statutory ban.

Under § 20(2) of Estonia's AML act (in force 21 July 2026) an obliged entity, to understand the purpose of a business relationship, must identify 'inter alia, the permanent seat, place of business or place of residence, profession or field of activity, main contracting partners, payment habits', whether the customer acts for another and, for a legal person, its experience. Banks' questionnaires on partners and payments trace to this clause (inference). The act does not require a 'connection with Estonia': the phrase occurs nowhere in its Estonian or English text (full-text search, 5 October 2026); § 10(4) only has a bank's board decide whether to serve persons from non-EEA countries.

  32. Supervision of Estonia's AML act is split by § 64 (in force 21 July 2026). The default supervisor is the Financial Intelligence Unit (Rahapesu Andmebüroo). Finantsinspektsioon supervises the credit and financial institutions under its financial supervision, in all their activities covered by the act. The Bar Association's board supervises attorneys; the Ministry of Justice and Digital Affairs, which may delegate to the Chamber of Notaries, supervises notaries. Applied: a bank or a payment institution licensed by Finantsinspektsioon answers to it, while a company-formation agent, an accountant or a financial institution authorised by the Unit itself (§ 70) answers to the Unit.

  33. To enforce a precept under Estonia's AML act the supervisor may impose a levy (§ 65). For a credit or financial institution that is a legal person: up to EUR 32,000 the first time and up to EUR 100,000 each further time for the same duty, in total not more than the higher of EUR 5,000,000 or 10 per cent of its annual turnover - amounts in the act since 27 November 2017 - or, added from 1 November 2023 (RT I, 17.03.2023, 2), twice the benefit derived from the breach or the harm prevented; for a legal person outside the financial sector up to EUR 32,000. The supervisor may inspect the place of business, examine documents without limitation and demand information without a visit (§ 66).

  34. Versobank's challenge to the loss of its licence failed in both EU courts. The European Central Bank replaced its decision of 26 March 2018 with one of 17 July 2018; on 6 October 2021 the General Court found no need to adjudicate on the first decision (T-351/18) and dismissed the action against the second (T-584/18); the Court of Justice dismissed Versobank AS's appeal on 7 September 2023 (C-803/21 P). The Court confirmed that, although Member States remain competent to apply anti-money-laundering rules, the ECB has exclusive competence to withdraw the authorisation of any credit institution, whatever its size - here on breaches that Finantsinspektsioon had found from 2015 on.

  38. Estonia's AML act lets a bank open an account before due diligence is complete in two cases (§ 27, in force 21 July 2026). An account may be opened before measures 1-3 of § 20(1) if no transaction can be made with the funds until they are applied. A credit institution may also open an account for a company being founded, on personal data verified automatically by the registrar or through a notary, provided the share-capital contribution arrives through an account at a credit institution operating in an EEA state, and the account is not debited before registration and measures 1-5; the representatives must conclude a settlement agreement within six months (§ 27(2), in force 1 February 2023).

Estonia's Financial Intelligence Unit can freeze money without a court order: under § 57 of the AML act (periods unchanged since the act took effect on 27 November 2017) it may, on suspicion of money laundering or terrorist financing, stop a transaction or restrict the disposal of an account or other property by a compliance notice for up to 30 calendar days, and for a further 60 calendar days where the possessor or owner fails to prove the legal origin of the property within the first 30 days or terrorist financing is suspected. Its information requests reach data under banking secrecy (§ 58(2)). An obliged entity reports a suspicion without delay, within two working days at most (§ 49(1)).

  44. Estonia's AML act lists risk-raising factors a bank must weigh (§ 37(2)-(3), in force 21 July 2026). Among them: the customer is a company with nominee shareholders or bearer shares; its ownership structure appears unusual or excessively complex; it is a cash-intensive business or a vehicle holding personal assets; the customer is a third-country national applying for residence rights or citizenship in Estonia in exchange for investment; and the relationship is started without meeting the customer or representative in person and without the § 31 remote-identification safeguard. The bank sets in its rules of procedure whether these factors apply as a whole, in part or as separate grounds.

Under § 65 of Estonia's Public Transport Act (wording in force 1 April 2026 - 31 January 2027, read 5 October 2026) a taxi driver whose rides are not ordered and priced through an information-society service must switch on a taximeter and give the passenger a printer-printed receipt showing the carrier's name and registry code, the number plate, date, start and end time, distance, prices used and the total; serving a passenger with a broken taximeter or printer is forbidden, and the passenger may refuse to pay if these duties are breached. For app-ordered rides the carrier gives a ride summary in a reproducible written form. The act has no rule on which means of payment a taxi must accept.

licensing 31

  1. A café that sells alcohol must have a cash register: Estonia's Alcohol Act § 44 (wording in force since 15 April 2004; consolidated text in force on 5 October 2026) permits retail sale of alcoholic drinks in a shop or a catering establishment only if a cash register is located at the place of business, through which every transaction in the retail sale of alcoholic drinks must be recorded. Not recording such a sale in the cash register is a misdemeanour: a fine of up to 200 fine units, for a legal person up to EUR 3,000 (§ 62). The act speaks of a cash register and sets no fiscal-memory or certification requirement. §§ 44 and 62 are unchanged in the text in force from 1 November 2026.

  5. Estonia's 2020 tightening of virtual-currency licensing: the Act amending the Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing Prevention Act and the State Fees Act, adopted 11 December 2019 (RT I, 31.12.2019, 2), in force from 10 March 2020. It merged exchange and wallet providers into 'virtual currency service providers', required the applicant's registered seat, management board and place of business to be in Estonia (or an Estonian-registered branch of a foreign company), a payment account with an EEA credit, e-money or payment institution serving Estonia, and share capital of at least EUR 12,000 paid in money; the application fee became EUR 3,300. Existing holders had to comply by 1 July 2020.

  7. Estonia's food supervision fee is set by statute. Under Food Act §§ 49^1-49^4 (text in force on 5 October 2026) a business that has notified or holds a licence pays an hourly fee for official controls: for the time spent on the supervision act but for no more than eight hours per act, counted to the half hour, travel time excluded (§ 49^3(3)); the minister sets the hourly rate for each year (§ 49^3(5)). For 2026 it is EUR 40.84 (regulation No 103 of 10 December 2025, RT I, 11.12.2025, 5, in force 1 January - 31 December 2026). The Board issues the payment decision by the seventh day of the month after the control, and the business pays within 28 days of receiving it (§ 49^4(1), (3)).

Supervision that follows is charged by the hour: EUR 40.84 in 2026, set by ministerial regulation No 103 of 10 December 2025 (RT I, 11.12.2025, 5).   22. A café in Estonia does not need a food licence in the ordinary case; it notifies. Food Act § 7(1) requires a notice of economic activities to the Agriculture and Food Board (Põllumajandus- ja Toiduamet) for handling food in an establishment under Article 6(2) of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004, with no state fee (§ 7(7)); an activity licence (§ 8) is reserved for listed cases such as establishments needing approval, retail handling of food of animal origin supplied to other retailers, and catering in kindergartens, schools, hospitals, care homes, prisons and the Defence Forces. The Board's page lists 'toitlustamine' (catering, including serving hot drinks) among activities to be notified.

  25. A café that serves alcohol files a second notice. Alcohol Act § 23(1) requires a notice of economic activities for selling alcohol in three fields of activity - retail trade, wholesale trade and catering - stating the place or places of business and the kinds of alcohol handled (§ 23(2)); the notice can be filed only through the Estonian information gateway (eesti.ee) or a notary (§ 23(3)). No notice is filed for selling alcohol at a public event (§ 23(1^1)). The local government - in Tallinn the city - supervises retail sale of alcoholic drinks on its territory (§ 49(4)) and its council may restrict it (§ 42).

  31. Estonia's licensing act for non-bank payment firms is the Payment Institutions and E-money Institutions Act (adopted 17 December 2009, in force 22 January 2010). A company needs an activity licence to act as a payment or e-money institution; Finantsinspektsioon grants and revokes it (§ 14(1), (3)); licences have no term and are not transferable (§ 14(4)). By Finantsinspektsioon's decision chapters 3, 4, 6 and 8 of the act do not apply to a payment institution if its average monthly payment volume over 12 months is at most EUR 3 million, it earns less than half its income from payments and it provides none of the services of § 3(1) points 6-8 (§ 11(2)); such a firm may not passport (§ 11(6)).

Since 1 January 2025 cash payments at physical points of sale in Estonia are rounded to the nearest five cents: up if the final price ends in 3, 4, 8 or 9 cents, down if it ends in 1, 2, 6 or 7 (§ 5-1 of the Act on the Introduction of the Euro and the Settlement of Cash Payments in Euros, inserted by RT I, 30.05.2024, 2). Card and other non-cash payments are not rounded, nor is a final price below three cents. The rule binds every trader and applies to payments by consumers, sole proprietors and representatives of legal persons; the Consumer Protection and Technical Regulatory Authority supervises it (§§ 5-3 to 5-5).

Price indication in Estonia is governed by §§ 7-8 of the Consumer Protection Act: when offering and selling goods a trader must make known to the consumer the selling price and the unit price - unless the regulation under § 7(8) provides otherwise for the unit price - in writing, clearly legible, unambiguous and easily noticeable (§ 7(1), (4)); the selling price is the final price the consumer pays (§ 7(2)); for a service the trader gives the final price or, where it cannot be fixed in advance, its components and basis of calculation, and displays a price list at the place of service or otherwise (§ 8). A price-reduction notice must show the earlier price (§ 7(6-1), since 28 May 2022).

  12. Estonian law obliges a merchant to accept cash, not cards. Under § 2(2) of the Act on the Introduction of the Euro and the Settlement of Cash Payments in Euros, persons other than Eesti Pank and credit institutions must accept up to 50 valid euro coins at a time and banknotes without limit, 'unless there is an agreement to use another means of payment' (wording in force since 1 March 2016). Refusal is a misdemeanour under § 74 of the Consumer Protection Act: up to 200 fine units, or up to EUR 40,000 for a legal person. No provision requiring a merchant to accept cards or other electronic payments was found in these two acts or in the payment chapters of the Law of Obligations Act.

  14. Estonia's general receipt rule is a consumer-law duty and prescribes no device. Under § 4(4) of the Consumer Protection Act (wording in force from 1 September 2025, RT I, 08.07.2025, 71) a trader must give the consumer a document proving the purchase when goods or services are paid for immediately; it must state at least the trader's name and address, the date, and each item's name, price and the amount paid (§ 4(4-1)). A paper document is given on request, and by default for a cash purchase without a loyalty card giving electronic access; it is not required where the consumer expressly agreed to receive it by e-mail or another channel (§ 4(4-2), (5-1)).

Wise pays only funds it has received from the scheme, may hold a rolling reserve, and asks before contracting about finances, activities, shareholders, beneficial owners, registered office and licences. Belgian law; courts of Belgium.

The bank pays the merchant within five settlement days of receiving the transaction notice (clause 23) and withholds chargebacks from payouts or debits the account (25). Art. 6(1) of Regulation (EU) No 910/2014 (eIDAS, consolidated version of 18 October 2024) obliges a Member State whose public-sector online service requires electronic identification to recognise an eID means issued in another Member State for cross-border authentication if (a) its scheme is on the Commission's published list, (b) its assurance level is substantial or high and at least the level the service requires, and (c) the public body itself uses level substantial or high for that service; recognition 'shall take place no later than 12 months after the Commission publishes the list'. Art. 6 covers authentication only; electronic signatures fall under its Arts 24a and 27.

Estonian law exempts start-ups from the EUR 65,000 investment and business-plan requirements of the residence permit for enterprise (Aliens Act § 192(2¹) 2), (6¹), in force since 18 January 2017) and provides a short- or long-stay visa for start-up entrepreneurship (§ 62⁴). A start-up is a business unit of a company registered in Estonia that is starting up and aims to develop and launch an innovative, repeatable business model with great global growth potential that contributes significantly to Estonia's business environment. Per the Police and Border Guard Board, an expert committee of the Ministry of the Interior evaluates the company within 10 working days of a complete application.

  3. A second enterprise route needs no residence in Estonia. Under Aliens Act § 197³(1) (text in force 1 October–31 December 2026) a large investor is an alien who has made a direct investment of at least EUR 1,000,000 in a company in the Estonian commercial register that invests mainly in the Estonian economy, or in an investment fund investing mainly in such companies; the investment must last for the permit's term (§ 197³(2)). § 197⁴ lifts the conditions of actual residence and of registering a residence in the population register; § 115 point 17 takes the permit out of the immigration quota. The Police and Border Guard Board's page gives a reply in 90 days and a permit of up to 5 years.

instant-payments 10

  1. Two dates circulate for the start of instant payments in Estonia. Eesti Pank's page on the payments market says 'The first Estonian banks joined the instant payment system in 2018', and its page on RT1 says that system, run by EBA Clearing, 'started work in November 2017'. The European Payments Council's participant register dates AS SEB Pank's readiness for SEPA Instant Credit Transfer to 21 November 2017, the scheme's first day, and Swedbank's and LHV Pank's to autumn 2018. So 2017 is the date of the first Estonian participant and 2018 the year the other two largest banks followed.

  2. Eurosystem central banks, Eesti Pank among them, do not hold client funds for payment or e-money institutions. Decision (EU) 2025/222 of the European Central Bank of 27 January 2025 (ECB/2025/2), applying from 9 April 2025, states in Article 3(1): 'Eurosystem central banks shall not offer or provide safeguarding accounts to NB-PSPs or to crypto-asset service providers.' Accounts that non-bank providers hold in central-bank-operated payment systems serve settlement and are capped by a maximum holding amount (Article 4). The date from which non-bank providers may request access to TARGET was moved from 16 June 2025 to 6 October 2025 by Decision (EU) 2025/1148 of 2 June 2025 (ECB/2025/18).

  4. SEPA migration in Estonia happened on 1 February 2014, the deadline of Regulation (EU) No 260/2012. Per Eesti Pank: from that date only the IBAN is officially used; it closed its retail payment system ESTA on 31 January 2014 and interbank payments moved to STEP2, with five settlement cycles a day instead of ten. The domestic direct debit gave way to the 'e-invoice standing order'. Its SEPA page (read 5 October 2026) says 'The banks operating in Estonia do not offer direct debit services'; its FAQ of early 2014 is narrower: banks do not let companies collect by SEPA direct debit within Estonia, while a bill abroad can be paid by cross-border SEPA direct debit from an Estonian account.

ubo-register 10

  1. Beneficial-owner filing by an Estonian company, as in force on 5 October 2026 (Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing Prevention Act §§ 76-77): an OÜ files, through the commercial register information system, each beneficial owner's name, personal identification code and its country (or date and place of birth and country of residence) and the manner of control; the data must be filed together with the application for entry in the commercial register; changes are filed within 30 days of learning of them; if nothing has changed, the company confirms the data when filing its annual report. The filing duty has applied since 1 September 2018.

  1. Estonian social tax (33%) is due on fees paid to a member of a management or controlling body of a legal person (Social Tax Act § 2(1) 4), § 7(1)), and the Tax and Customs Board applies it to a non-resident board member too: social tax 'is not due on remuneration paid to members of the management body of an Estonian company only if the recipient of such remuneration has been issued in his or her home country a certificate of social security coverage valid in such foreign country on Form A1' (page updated 4 November 2025). The company must also register the paid board member in the employment register.

psd2 7

  1. The legislative history confirms that Estonia kept its surcharge ban at the PSD2 minimum. The Government's explanatory memorandum to bill 498 SE - the 2017 act transposing PSD2, which added § 725(9) to the Law of Obligations Act - summarises the change as a ban on charging an additional fee for the use of '(most)' card-based payment instruments and states that the ban does not extend to payment cards whose fees are not regulated in Chapter II of Regulation (EU) 2015/751: 'such payment instruments are commercial cards'. The memorandum does not discuss using the Member State option of Article 62(5) of PSD2 to prohibit or limit surcharges more widely.

  2. Estonia did not extend the surcharge ban beyond what PSD2 itself requires. For instruments outside § 725(9) of the Law of Obligations Act - in practice commercial cards and three-party schemes - § 725(7) says the contract between the payee and its payment service provider 'may provide for' the right to agree a fee with the payer or offer a discount for a particular payment instrument. Since 15 July 2025 a second sentence caps that fee at the payee's actual cost of using the instrument (added by the act of 18 June 2025, RT I, 08.07.2025, 4). Under § 725(8) a payer not told of the fee before initiating the payment owes nothing.

The Law of Obligations Act draws the line at 'consumer': under § 733^14(6) (wording of RT I, 01.03.2023, 3, in force 11 March 2023), where the client 'is not a consumer' the parties may agree that §§ 710^1-711^2 (duty to contract, information), 719^1 (two months' notice of changes), 720 (cancellation), the second sentence of § 724^1(2), § 725(5), §§ 726-727^1, 733^3, 733^4 (burden of proof), 733^6 (refunds) and 733^8 (payer's liability) do not apply in part or in full, and may agree a period other than the 13 months of § 733^7(2) for reporting unauthorised payments. The act has no word for micro-enterprise.

vat 7

  1. An Estonian company with no business in Estonia may be refused VAT registration. Under § 20(4¹) of the Value-Added Tax Act (in force since 1 March 2014; text as of 5 October 2026) a person must prove, to be registered, that it engages in or is starting business in Estonia; the tax authority may ask for more evidence, decides within five working days of receiving it, and does not register a person who neither engages in nor starts business. The Tax and Customs Board's page for companies founded by e-residents (updated 4 November 2025, read 5 October 2026) says Estonian businesses 'are not automatically deemed value added tax payers'.

audit 6

  1. Compulsory review (ülevaatus) of annual accounts in Estonia, as in force on 5 October 2026 (Auditors Activities Act § 92(1)-(3)): a review is compulsory where at least two of these are exceeded - sales revenue or income EUR 2,000,000, total assets EUR 1,000,000, average number of employees 24 - or at least one of these - EUR 6,000,000, EUR 3,000,000, 72 employees; a compulsory review may be replaced by an audit. The euro amounts were set by Act RT I, 07.01.2025, 1 (in force 17 January 2025) and apply to reporting periods that began from 1 January 2024. An OÜ below the review thresholds has no statutory audit or review duty unless its articles or another law impose one.

deposit-guarantee 5

  1. The Estonian Guarantee Fund (Tagatisfond) lists eight credit institutions whose deposits it guarantees (page last edited 04/06/2025): AS Inbank, AS LHV Pank, AS SEB Pank, Bigbank AS, Coop Pank AS, Holm Bank AS, Luminor Bank AS and Swedbank AS. Its FAQ states that 'deposits of both private individuals and businesses are compensated, with the exception of deposits not subject to compensation', and that it does not guarantee deposits in the Estonian branch of a credit institution of another European Economic Area state, which fall under the home state's scheme. A deposit whose disposal the Financial Intelligence Unit has restricted is compensated only after the precept is revoked.

  3. Deposits in Estonian banks are guaranteed by the Guarantee Fund. Under § 25(2) of the Guarantee Fund Act (text in force from 21 July 2026) eligible deposits are compensated with accrued interest up to EUR 100,000 per depositor in any one credit institution; a natural person gets up to a further EUR 100,000 for sums credited in the previous six months from a home sale and listed life events (§ 25(2^1)). Payment is completed within seven working days of the date deposits become unavailable; its supervisory board may extend this by up to ten working days in extraordinary circumstances (§ 41(2)). A company's deposit is covered unless the company is one of the excluded entities of § 30.

  2. Paysera opens a business account for an Estonian company in its app. Per its Estonian pages (read 5 October 2026) the head of the company, or a person with a power of attorney e-signed by the head or certified by a notary, first verifies their own identity, then completes a KYC questionnaire; 'one of the required documents is the list of shareholders'. Companies registered in Lithuania, Latvia, Estonia, Bulgaria or Romania use the app; those registered elsewhere file documents in a browser. For a company registered in a SEPA country that is not an 'international company', opening is free and administration EUR 5 a month; an 'international company' pays EUR 100 and EUR 20 a month.

employment 2

  1. Before a café's first employee starts, the employer enters the start of work in the employment register (Taxation Act, text in force on 5 October 2026): under § 25^2 the person providing work is the obliged person, registers commencement 'no later than the moment the person starts work', and registers suspension and termination within ten days. § 25^1(4) covers, among others, persons working under an employment contract, persons providing services under a contract under the law of obligations (except a sole proprietor and a payer of business income tax), and members of a legal person's management or controlling body, where their work gives rise to a tax liability in Estonia.

  2. Estonia's employment register, kept by the Tax and Customs Board, as in force on 5 October 2026: the person providing work, resident or non-resident, registers the start of work no later than the moment work starts, and a suspension or termination within ten days (Taxation Act § 25²). Entered are natural persons 'whose working gives rise to a tax liability in Estonia': employees, persons serving under a contract under the law of obligations (except sole proprietors and entrepreneur-account holders) and members of a legal person's management or controlling body (§ 25¹(4) p 1-3). Penalty payments are capped at EUR 3,300 in total - EUR 1,300 the first time, EUR 2,000 the second (§ 25⁸(3)).

  1. Strong customer authentication in Estonian law took effect on 14 September 2019, not with the rest of the PSD2 transposition: § 5(2) of the transposing Act (RT I, 07.12.2017, 1) put the Law of Obligations Act provisions on it (§ 724^4(5) and (8), § 724^5(3), § 724^6, § 727^1(5)) into force 18 months after the Commission's technical standard entered into force, and Finantsinspektsioon's circular of 3 December 2020 dates Delegated Regulation (EU) 2018/389 as in force 14 March 2018 and applied from 14 September 2019. For card payments in e-commerce the circular follows the European Banking Authority: the extra migration period ended on 31 December 2020.
